masthead.headline: Motion reads as cheap for two reasons, and both of them are numbers you can name.
masthead.lede: This board teaches one concept end to end: how long a thing takes, and how it distributes that time. By the end you should be able to say what is wrong with an animation in words a motion designer would recognise, instead of saying it feels off.

sections.label: The model
sections.title: Every piece of interface motion is these four decisions.

points.lead: Duration is a budget, not a taste.
points.text: Most interface motion belongs between 150ms and 300ms. Under 100ms it is not perceived as motion; over 400ms the reader is waiting for the software.

points.lead: Easing is where that budget is spent.
points.text: The same 220ms feels mechanical spread evenly and deliberate spent mostly at the start. Linear is the giveaway: nothing in the physical world moves at a constant speed from rest.

points.lead: Entrances and exits are not symmetrical.
points.text: Something arriving should decelerate into place so the eye can follow it. Something leaving should accelerate away, because nobody needs to watch it go.

blocks.text: Work through the four in order. Each one is a question with a defensible answer, and skipping any of them is what produces motion that technically animates and still reads as an afterthought.

items.title: Decide what the motion is for
items.text: Motion answers exactly one of: where did this come from, what just changed, or is the system still working. If it answers none of those, the right duration is zero.

items.title: Set the duration from the distance
items.text: A small element moving a short way needs less time than a full-screen sheet. 150ms for a toggle or a chip; 200 to 250ms for a card or a menu; up to 350ms for something crossing the whole viewport.

items.title: Choose the curve from the direction
items.text: Arriving takes ease-out, so it lands softly. Leaving takes ease-in, so it commits and goes. Something both leaving and arriving — a page transition — takes ease-in-out.

items.title: Check it against the reader who did not ask for it
items.text: Play it ten times in a row, then honour prefers-reduced-motion. Motion that is pleasant once and irritating on the tenth repeat is too long, not too fast.

sections.label: The words
sections.title: Six terms, and the sentence each one lets you say.

blocks.text: The point of the vocabulary is not precision for its own sake. It is that a named cause can be fixed by someone else, and “feels cheap” cannot. Each entry below gives the meaning, then the phrasing that gets the change made.

detail: How the motion's time is distributed across its distance, written as a timing function. Say:

detail.text: this is on a linear curve; put it on ease-out so it decelerates into place

detail: Fast at the start, slow at the end. The default for anything arriving, because the eye catches it early and then has time to read where it stopped. Say:

detail.text: entrances should be ease-out, not linear

detail: Slow at the start, fast at the end. Correct for exits and wrong for entrances, where it reads as hesitation. Say:

detail.text: the dismissal should ease in and get out of the way

detail: The total time, in milliseconds. Quote it as a number, always. Say:

detail.text: this is running at 500ms; it wants about 220

detail: — which is a change anyone can make, unlike “it's too slow”.
A fixed delay applied between siblings so a list arrives in sequence rather than as a block. Say:

detail.text: stagger the rows by about 30ms so the list reads top to bottom

detail: . Above roughly 60ms it stops reading as one gesture.
Motion described by stiffness and damping rather than by a curve and a clock, so it can overshoot and settle. Say:

detail.text: this wants a spring, not a curve — it should overshoot slightly and settle

detail: . Reach for it when something is being grabbed or thrown, not for a menu.

rows.text: It's on a linear curve — put the entrance on ease-out
Bring it from 400ms to 200ms and keep the curve
One number, and the rest is held still
The rows all arrive at once; stagger them by 30ms
It's fine once and tiring on the tenth repeat — halve it
Says which viewing it fails on
Overshoot slightly and settle, rather than stopping dead
Turns a mood into a behaviour

sections.label: Feel it
sections.title: The same distance, twice, with only the numbers changed.

blocks.text: Both panels below travel exactly the same distance. The left one is fixed at linear over 500ms — the shape almost every unconsidered animation has, because it is what you get by typing a number and moving on. Set the right one yourself, play them together, and watch which one you stop noticing.

blocks.title: Easing and duration, side by side
blocks.alt: Two panels slide in from the left inside their own frames. The left is fixed at a linear curve over 500 milliseconds. The right takes a curve chosen from linear, ease-in, ease-out and ease-in-out, and a duration set on a slider between 80 and 800 milliseconds, defaulting to ease-out at 220. A Play both button replays them together, and a readout names the current pairing.

blocks.text: Two things are worth trying deliberately. Put the right panel on ease-in and play it: an entrance that starts slowly reads as the software thinking. Then take the duration to 800ms on any curve — the motion is smooth, correct, beautifully eased, and still wrong, which is the demonstration that the curve cannot rescue the clock.

sections.label: Check it
sections.title: What to look for before you sign it off.

blocks.label: Checks you will actually run
blocks.ask: Which of these will you run on the next animation you review?

options.value: It answers one of the three questions
options.summary: Where it came from, what changed, or that the system is working — otherwise cut it.

options.value: The duration is in the 150–300ms band
options.summary: Or has a stated reason for being outside it, such as distance travelled.

options.value: Entrances ease out, exits ease in
options.summary: And nothing that arrives is on a linear curve.
Judged on the tenth viewing, not the first.
The state change still happens; only the travel between states is dropped.

blocks.label: Naming the fault out loud
blocks.ask: After the demo, how confident are you naming what is wrong with an animation in a review?

sections.label: Ask for it
sections.title: Two requests a motion designer can act on without a meeting.

blocks.text: The test of the vocabulary is whether a request written in it can be implemented by someone who was not in the conversation. Both prompts below pass that test: each names the element, the property, the number, and what it should look like when it is right.

blocks.caption: A review comment, written in the vocabulary
blocks.code:
The settings panel entrance is on a linear curve at 500ms.

Put it on ease-out and bring it to 220ms — it should decelerate into place rather than arriving at a constant speed. Keep the exit as it is; that one is already ease-in and reads fine.

The rows inside the panel all land together. Stagger them by 30ms so the list reads top to bottom, and cap the total at about 200ms so a long list does not turn into a queue.

blocks.caption: A brief, before anything is built
blocks.code:
Dragging a card between columns should feel grabbed rather than transported.

Use a spring rather than a curve: slight overshoot on drop, settling within about 400ms. Everything else on this board stays on ease-out at 200ms, so the drag is the only place anything overshoots — that contrast is the point.

Under prefers-reduced-motion the card still moves columns; it just arrives without travel.

blocks.label: The animation you are going to fix
blocks.ask: Name one animation in your own product and write the request in these words.
blocks.placeholder: For example: the toast slides up over 600ms on ease-in-out. Put it on ease-out at 200ms; it should arrive and settle, not drift in and drift back out.
